newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma media says many dissatisfied with Suu Kyi.
newsitem.headline: Burma media says many dissatisfied with Suu Kyi.

text.p: Burmese state-run newspapers said on Tuesday it was difficult to say who was behind weekend attacks on democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi's motorcade because she has caused trouble for so many people.
"Suu Kyi will get into trouble if she thinks that every group she sees is her supporters," a commentary run in official newspapers said.
"It is difficult to allege specifically who are opposed to Suu Kyi, for Suu Kyi has caused trouble to various strata of society."

The commentary, written by a regular columnist who goes by the penname "Byatti" but who is thought by many in Rangoon to be a senior military officer, recounted the official version of events leading to Saturday's attacks on Suu Kyi's motorcade.
It says about 200 people opposed to the Nobel Peace laureate threw stones at the motorcade, cracking several windows and windshields of different cars in the convoy.
Suu Kyi, who emerged unhurt from the incident, blamed the government for orchestrating the two attacks and filed an official complaint with police.
A government official told Reuters the attacks were acts of sabotage from which the government had nothing to gain. He said authorities had launched an inquiry.

Diplomats said there was no doubt the government was involved. They said on Saturday there were about 2,000 young men near Suu Kyi's house, most of whom had been paid by the government to come in from neighbouring townships to cause unrest.
They were the ones who attacked Suu Kyi's car, witnesses and diplomats said.
The newspaper commentary said there were many people who had suffered from Suu Kyi's outspoken attacks against the government.

Since her release from six years of house arrest in July 1995, Suu Kyi has urged foreigners not to invest in Burma until the military government improves its human rights records and takes steps towards a return to democracy.
She has also said she favours economic sanctions against Burma.

"As Suu Kyi is becoming more and more apparent as the one trying to destroy...prospects for stability of the state with her fangs, it is rather difficult to definitely indicate what sorts of people do not want her," the newspaper commentary said.

Suu Kyi, daughter of Burma's independence hero Aung San, is the leader of the opposition National League for Democracy which won May 1990 general elections in a landslide, a victory the military rulers refused to recognise.
